text:
**For most full-size fridges, a station with about 1,000–1,500 Wh of battery and at least 1,800 W of continuous output gets you through about a day. Get about 2,000 Wh or more if you want real margin or plan to run other things too.**

## The three things to check

**1. Running watts (easy).** A full-size fridge draws about 100–250 W while the compressor runs. Almost any 1,000 W-class station handles that. ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))

**2. Startup surge (where most stations fail).** The compressor briefly spikes to several times its running draw when it starts. Estimates for this spike vary:
- About 900–1,200 W for modern fridges ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- Up to 1,500–2,400 W for large French-door or older fridges ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))

Some brands' advertised surge numbers only apply to simple loads like heaters, not motors ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). To be safe, pick a station whose *continuous* rating is around 1,800 W or more. Also make sure it has pure sine wave output, which all major LiFePO4 brands do.

**3. Battery capacity (Wh) decides how long it runs.** A fridge's compressor only runs part of the time, so its average draw is much lower than its running watts. To estimate yours:
- Find the yellow EnergyGuide label and divide the kWh/year figure by 8.76. That gives average watts.
- A typical 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge uses 362 kWh/yr, which works out to about **41 W average**.
- Over 24 hours, after inverter losses and 20% headroom, that's about **1,400 Wh per day**. ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator))
- Large side-by-sides with ice makers can use about twice that.

## Rough runtimes by size
(From [HomeGrid HQ's table](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))

| Class | Example | Approx. fridge runtime | Price |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~770 Wh | Bluetti AC70 | ~12 hrs | $359 |
| ~1,000 Wh | Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, Anker SOLIX C1000 | ~17 hrs | $470–499 |
| ~2,000 Wh | Bluetti AC200L / Elite 200 V2, EcoFlow Delta 3 Max | ~33 hrs | $879–899 |
| ~3,000 Wh | Bluetti Elite 300, OUPES Mega 3 | ~2 days | $1,199 |

## A good all-around pick: Bluetti AC200L (2,048 Wh)
- 2,400 W continuous output, LiFePO4 battery, 5-year warranty
- Expandable to 8 kWh with add-on batteries, so you can buy one day of runtime now and add more later
- **Buy:** [https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) (goes to Bluetti's official US store)
- Listed at $899. Dealectric says code **AFF5OFF** brought it to $854.05 when they tested it on Oct 21. ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l))
- Disclosure: this is an affiliate link, and Dealectric earns a commission. The code and price come from their own testing, so the store's checkout has the final word.
- Dealectric also notes that the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 costs the same and is rated for more charge cycles (6,000+ vs. 3,000+), but it isn't expandable.

On a budget, a ~1,000 Wh unit like the Jackery 1000 v2 or Anker C1000 (about $470–499) covers most of a day. My search results didn't include direct store links for those, but you can find them via "Check price" on [HomeGrid HQ's comparison](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).

## Tips
- Keep the fridge door shut. Food becomes unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F. ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- Test the station with your actual fridge before an outage to confirm it handles the startup surge.
- For multi-day outages, look for strong solar input. The AC200L accepts up to 1,200 W.

If you share your fridge's kWh/year from its EnergyGuide label and how long your outages usually last, I can narrow down the exact size.
